passage: In the summer holidays I stopped having any times at all. I stayed up late watching videos with my brother Lalit, woke up at noon and ate breakfast at lunchtime. By the third week I was grumpy all day and my head felt fuzzy. Then Mummy said school starts on Monday, and my stomach went tight. I didn't want to go back. Mummy didn't shout. She said, "Let's pick two things that stay the same every day." We chose waking up at eight and playing outside after lunch. The first mornings were horrible. But by Sunday I felt more like me, and Monday was only a little scary. My name is Gurleen, and next holidays I'm keeping the two things.

qa.q: What two things did Gurleen and Mummy choose?
qa.a: Waking up at eight and playing outside after lunch.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when Mummy said school starts on Monday?
qa.a: Gurleen felt dread; the stomach went tight and there was no wish to go back.

qa.q: Why did picking two fixed things help?
qa.a: Simple anchors like a wake time and outdoor play brought back a rhythm, so Gurleen felt more normal and Monday was less scary.

qa.q: What might Mummy have noticed about Gurleen during the holidays?
qa.a: Mummy likely saw Gurleen grumpy and fuzzy-headed from late nights, and chose a calm plan over shouting.

grounding: A child's holiday of late nights and no fixed times leaves the child grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors smooth the return.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, first week after the Puja holidays. Ramesh Dutta.
Arnab came back yawning, pale and short-tempered. On Monday he put his head on the desk during reading and snapped at his partner. When I asked gently, he said, "I slept at two every night. I watched videos. Now I hate mornings and I hate school." He looked close to tears.
I didn't lecture. I asked Arnab to choose one thing that could help this week. He chose lights-off at a fixed time and football at recess instead of sitting inside. I phoned his mother that evening, and she agreed to back him up. By Friday he was joking with his partner again.
Next year I'll send families a note before the holidays: keep one wake time and some outdoor play.

qa.q: What time did Arnab say he slept every night?
qa.a: Arnab slept at two every night.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling on Monday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Arnab felt tired, grumpy and close to tears, saying he hated mornings and school.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do instead of lecturing?
qa.a: Ramesh asked Arnab to choose a helpful change, a fixed lights-off time and football at recess, and phoned home so his mother could back him up.

qa.q: How might Arnab's reading partner have experienced Monday?
qa.a: The partner was snapped at and probably felt confused or hurt, not knowing Arnab was simply exhausted.

grounding: A child's late-night, screen-filled holiday leaves him grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors like a sleep time and outdoor play ease the return.
